nodes.title: HIPAA evidence for Supabase: RLS, functions, views, triggers and audit logs as pgTAP tests
nodes.body: From the team behind [rlsautotest](https://github.com/unitautogen/rlsautotest) (featured in Supabase’s July 2026 Developer Update): `unitautogen hipaa `generates pgTAP tests and seed data from RLS policies, security definer functions, views, triggers and audit tables to prove, per tenant and identity, who can read, write or tamper with PHI - and maps the result to HIPAA 164.312. Supabase signs the BAA and secures the platform. By their own [HIPAA guidance](https://supabase.com/docs/guides/security/hipaa-compliance), applying the recommended database controls responsibility falls to the customer, and those controls are the part a HIPAA review actually asks about. How to run it ``` bash supabase start unitautogen --supabase hipaa --schema public ``` Tests land in supabase/tests/, so supabase test db and CI re-run them on every migration. It runs on the local stack, built from the migrations, so no patient data is involved. **What it proves** - **Access**: run as each role and called as two tenants: RLS, security definer functions, views (catches a view without security_invoker), triggers and column grants. A failing test is the proof of a leak. - **Storage**: who can read and list a bucket’s files. - **Audit**: every insert, update and delete on a PHI table leaves a row recording who did it - and a client can’t forge or delete that row. - **Branches**: data is seeded for every branch of each function, trigger and view, not just the happy path. Multi-tenant and RBAC patterns included. **What it maps to** The evidence is organized by the Technical Safeguards under **45 CFR 164.312:** - **164.312(a)(1)** Access Control - RLS, security definer functions, views and column grants, run per tenant and identity. Proof that access to PHI is restricted to the right rows and the right roles. - **164.312(b)** Audit Controls - every insert, update and delete on a PHI table is recorded with the actor who made it. - **164.312(c)(1)** Integrity - PHI changes are controlled and audit rows cannot be forged or deleted, so the record of what happened holds up. - **164.312(d)** Person or Entity Authentication - the database-side half: access is bound to the authenticated role or identity. How the login itself is verified sits outside the database and is flagged as not the tool’s responsibility. - Transmission security, 164.312(e), is encryption in transit and stays out of scope. **What does the report give-** One per schema: - Each safeguard above marked gap found or no gaps found. - A What to fix list, one row per object, with the exact SQL change per gap. - Every finding linked to its pgTAP test, ready to commit and re-run. - A SHA-256 stamp over the report and every test behind it. Edit the report and it stops matching. **UnitAutogen** works on any Postgres - Supabase, Neon, RDS, self-hosted. The HIPAA report is in the Enterprise edition (free trial, reduced rate for Supabase startups). If you run Supabase for healthcare, I’d like your feedback on where it helps and where it misses. Docs: https://unitautogen.com/postgresql/unitautogen/docs/hipaa/ Download-https://github.com/unitautogen/unitautogen-postgresql/releases

nodes.title: Impact of Loki 429 Errors on All Tenants in a Shared Vector Pipeline
nodes.body:
We are experiencing issues where a 429 (Too Many Requests) error from Grafana Loki is impacting all tenants in a shared Vector pipeline. This happens when one of our tenants generates a high volume of logs, which leads to throttling or rate-limiting on Loki's ingester. The problem is that all tenants in the same Vector pipeline are affected, even though logs are isolated by tenant via the X-Scope-OrgID header.

I thought that adding the `X-Scope-OrgID` header in the request would isolate the batch request for each tenant. Is that correct?

When one of the tenants gets a 429 error, how does Vector.dev behave for other tenants in the shared Vector pipeline?

Assuming the impact on all tenants is correct behavior in one vector pipeline, and I know that one of the tenants in my Vector pipeline will get a 429 error, what is the best configuration for this scenario? should i seperate the sinks? or should i seperate the vectors or etc

I would appreciate it ifyou could help me figure this out.

nodes.title: What can an agent actually do with fastmcp, and who decides?
nodes.body:
I maintain an open-source project called mnki that puts a verification step in front of an MCP `tools/call`, so a client can see what an agent was authorised to do before the server runs it. I'm not selling anything today; I'm trying to find out whether "which server can do what, for whom" is a real problem for people who publish servers, or whether I've invented it.

One line in your README stood out to me: "[Upgrading from MCP SDK v1](https://gofastmcp.com/getting-started/upgrading/from-mcp-sdk-v1) or [v2](https://gofastmcp.com/getting-started/upgrading/from-mcp-sdk-v2)". That is the closest thing I have seen to an answer inside the server itself, and I would like to understand where it stops.

If you have 20 minutes I'd like to hear how you think about it and what users ask you. If it's easier to try than to talk: `npx mnki-cli scan` lists every MCP server configured on a machine and `mnki protect --mode observe` records what *would* have been denied without changing anything (https://mnki.com/docs/integrations).

Either way, thank you for fastmcp.

nodes.title: File Metadata and Filtering
nodes.body:
Hi

I currently have a Qdrant vector database in production. I am thinking about switching over to RAG-Anything. I am curious if RAG-Anything has support for attaching metadata to Files/chunks/nodes at ingestion time. The reason for these metadata fields are to allow the search to be filtered. These metadata Key Value (KV's) pairs would allow us to restrict data to what users are allowed to see and also provide the agent with more information about the file. For instance, in Qdrant I attach roles and file_paths to the metadata, so that I can control file access via RBAC and then also provide the file_path to my agent so it can directly pull files from our virtual file system (VFS) via VFS tools.

Does anyone have insight into if this is currently supported or if it is planned to be supported? It would need to be supported for both the vector database and graph nodes.

nodes.title: Personal scopes per user + tenant-owned SSO (multi-tenant use case)
nodes.body:
*Design sketch, based on reading the code at `root` 25b5649; nothing below is implemented yet.*

## Why

We run ctx as a shared knowledge layer for several tenants (one per customer or person). The next tenant is a company with its own OIDC IdP. What they need:

1. Every employee gets a **personal scope** that only they can read, plus read access to the company's **shared knowledge** (written by a curator group).
2. Onboarding through **their SSO**, without an operator minting keys and linking identities by hand.
3. Their tools (MCP clients, agents) connect through the **SSO session**, without anyone pasting a raw key.
4. Background pipelines (dream, digest, root map, guard) stay **clean between users**: nothing from a personal scope ends up in another user's links, prompts, digests or maps.

Most building blocks already exist: OIDC login, E4b admin-invite, per-key `home_scope`/`allowed_scopes`/`write_scopes`, Model C, the OAuth AS with `ctxt_` tokens, scope-pure topics, and the same-scope gates in dream (V5). What is missing is mostly *knowing which scope is personal*, plus the tenant side of SSO.

## One rule for everything

**I-FLOW:** for every LLM call and every persisted artefact, `readers(output scope) ⊆ ⋂ readers(input scopes)`.
Shared scope = all tenant members; personal scope = its owner. A per-user digest over `{own personal} ∪ shared`, written into the personal scope, is fine. A tenant digest over a window that contains personal scopes, written into a shared scope, is not.

## Proposed building blocks (each opt-in; defaults keep today's behaviour byte-identical)

**A. Scope kind + owner (foundation).** Two columns on `context_tenant_scopes`: `kind` (`shared` default | `personal`) and `owner_principal_id` (NULL unless personal), with `CHECK ((kind='personal') = (owner IS NOT NULL))` and one personal scope per (tenant, principal). Enforced at key mint/update: a personal scope may only appear in a key's scopes if the key's principal owns it. `tenant-grant-create` refuses personal scopes.

**B. Background windows derived from the register.**
- `scheduler.read_scopes` becomes a *narrowing* of `owned` (unset = all owned). The default tenant stays as it is.
- Dream: the pick window is the tenant's scopes, the candidate window is `visible(block.scope)` (personal → own + shared, shared → shared). Phase 1 keeps links same-scope, so this only fixes recall. Personal→shared links (`topical`/`factual` only, never `supersedes`) are a separate, later question.
- Digest and root map: per target (one shared layer per tenant, one per personal scope). `RunDigest`/`rootmap.Run` already take home and window separately, so only the scheduler loop changes.
- Guard: the candidate set becomes the visible set of the checked block, and cross-scope hits are flagged, not archived (touches #185).
- Audit/classify: iterate all owned scopes, not only the home scope.

**C. Tenant-owned OIDC providers** (the deferred 066/L6 seam; new migration since 066 is folded):
- `tenant_id` on `context_oauth_providers`.
- Identities bound to the provider row (`provider_id` + partial unique indexes; legacy rows unchanged).
- A tenant ceiling on web sessions, so `PickPrincipalKey`/key-select can never land on another tenant's key.
- `oauth-provider-*` usable by tenant-admins with in-handler isolation and restricted fields (`oidc` only, `allowed_claim` mandatory, no URL overrides).
- Audit entities for providers and identities.

**D. Opt-in JIT provisioning per provider** (`provisioning: invite | jit`; `invite` stays the default, so E4b is unchanged unless an operator opts in):
- On the first login, one transaction creates the principal, the personal scope and a `member` key (reads the shared scopes; `write_scopes` only if the curator claim matches).
- Claims are re-evaluated on every login. Never link by email; JIT requires a non-empty `allowed_claim`.
- Offboarding means key-level deactivation inside the tenant; the data stays.

**E. Session-based consent at `/authorize`.** This is an extra branch; the key-entry path stays byte-identical for existing connectors.
- With a valid session, the consent screen shows tenant, key and scopes. The POST is bound to the session's CSRF secret.
- Each tool gets a **child key** (same principal and tenant, scopes ⊆ the parent's). Tokens can then be narrower than the user without making `token.scope` authoritative, so INV-B stays intact.
- "My connected tools" list plus self-revoke under `/api/session/*`.

**F. Principal overview** (read-only manage action): identities, keys of *this* tenant, token aggregates per client, last login, effective status. Tenant-filtered for tenant-admins.

## How we would deliver

We build the whole thing in our fork and test it end to end against a real IdP. Upstream it arrives as **one PR**, only after the complete feature works. Inside it, each block A–F is its own commit, so it can be read block by block. Every block has tests that are red on `root` and green with the change, and docs ship with each block.

## Questions before we start

1. Is opt-in JIT acceptable upstream at all, given E4b's "no auto-create" decision? (Default stays `invite`.)
2. Is `context_tenant_scopes` the right home for kind/owner? Should personal be strictly owner-only, including for tenant owners and admins?
3. Do you accept `scheduler.read_scopes` as a narrowing of `owned` (unset = all owned)?
4. Personal→shared dream links: wanted at all? If yes, `topical`/`factual` only?
5. Tenant-owned providers: lower `oauth-provider-*` to the tenant-admin tier, or separate `tenant-oauth-provider-*` actions? Did "L6" contain anything you want preserved?
6. Session consent: limit it to admin-registered or statically trusted clients (DCR `open` excluded)? Child key, or something else, for narrower tool rights?
7. Re-checking claims at refresh: store the IdP refresh token sealed (`offline_access`), or enforce a periodic re-login per provider?
8. Coordination: B overlaps #185, #199/#214, #228 and #231. Should we wait for those, or fold the scope-kind predicate into them? Once the direction is settled, should this become one tracking issue before the PR?

We have a detailed gap analysis with file/function references for every point above and can share it.

nodes.title: Schema อธิบายแบบสั้น — สามชั้น, column idiom, composite FK, และคำถามเรื่องการลืม
nodes.body:
อธิบาย schema แบบสั้น สำหรับคนที่ต้องแก้มันจริง ไม่ใช่คนอ่านผ่าน

`SPEC.md` §3 คือของจริง โพสต์นี้คือทางลัด · การออกแบบที่ยังเปิดอยู่คุยที่ #12

## โครงสร้าง — สามชั้น ชั้นเดียวกันหมด

v4 ไม่ได้ออกแบบ schema ใหม่ ชั้นล่างสุดคือของ Honcho ทั้งดุ้น ชั้นบนเป็นของ v3 ที่เขียนใหม่ให้หน้าตาเหมือนชั้นล่าง

```
bank = workspaces            alias เดียวในระบบ ไม่มีตาราง `banks` ไม่มีคอลัมน์ `bank_id`
  │  FK ทุกตัวชี้ที่ workspaces.name  ไม่ใช่ id
  │
  ├── TIER 1 · Honcho ของแท้ byte-compatible ──── honcho/src/models.py
  │     peers               name = 'm5:arra-oracle-v3'  (federation tag ทั้งก้อน รวม host)
  │     sessions            is_active BOOL  -- สองสถานะ ใช้บิตเดียว
  │     session_peers       joined_at / left_at  -- ออกจากห้องคือ timestamp ไม่ใช่ DELETE
  │     messages            UNIQUE (workspace_name, session_name, seq_in_session)
  │                         +v4  role · in_reply_to · read · read_at   (NULL ได้ทุกตัว)
  │
  ├── TIER 2 · memory จาก arra-oracle-v3 ─────────────────────── §3.4
  │     memories            15 คอลัมน์ + 2 JSON bag
  │       │                 created_at | valid_from -> valid_to   (bitemporal)
  │       │                 superseded_by ──┐
  │       │                 <───────────────┘  supersede ไม่ delete
  │       └── memory_terms ──> terms ──> vocabularies   (taxonomy ทรง Drupal)
  │     supersede_log       workspace_name NOT NULL  -- รูที่ v3 เปิดไว้
  │
  └── TIER 3 · activity ──────────────────────────────────────── §14
        traces              parent_id (tree) + prev_id (sequence) = กราฟ
          └── distilled_to ──> memories       raw -> distilled -> retired
        mcp_calls           workspace_name NOT NULL  (§6.3)
        connections         §7.2
```

Tier 1 export ออกมาแล้ว import เข้า Honcho ตัวจริงได้เลย — คอลัมน์ที่ v4 เพิ่มเป็น `NULL` ได้ทุกตัว

## Column idiom — ตารางใหม่ทุกตัวต้องหน้าตาแบบนี้

Honcho ทั้งห้าตารางใช้ shape เดียวกัน v4 เอา shape นั้นมาใช้กับตารางของตัวเองด้วย ไม่ใช่แค่ tier 1

```
id                 TEXT PK nanoid(21)
name               TEXT                     -- UNIQUE (name, workspace_name)
workspace_name     TEXT NOT NULL            -- FK -> workspaces.name
h_metadata         JSON                     -- user-visible
internal_metadata  JSON                     -- internal
created_at         TIMESTAMP
FK (x_name, workspace_name) -> x (name, workspace_name)   -- composite เสมอ
```

กฎตัดสินว่าอะไรเป็นคอลัมน์ อะไรลง JSON: **filter key หรือ display field**

| | |
|---|---|
| ใช้ `WHERE` ด้วย | เป็นคอลัมน์จริง — libSQL กับ Lance push predicate ลงคอลัมน์ ลง JSON ไม่ได้ |
| แค่เอาไปแสดงผล | ลง `h_metadata` |

กฎข้อนี้ทำให้ `memories` เหลือ 15 คอลัมน์ จาก 21

## Composite FK — isolation ที่ database บังคับเอง ไม่ใช่โค้ดบังคับ

จุดนี้สำคัญที่สุดในทั้ง schema ทุก FK ข้ามตารางพา tenant ไปด้วยเสมอ

```sql
FK (session_name, workspace_name) -> sessions (name, workspace_name)
   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^  tenant อยู่ "ใน" key
```

อ้างข้าม bank = constraint violation ตอน INSERT ไม่ใช่ assert ที่ runtime

v3 ใช้ assert แล้วมีรูสองรู ทั้งคู่ **fail open** — คือพัง แล้วคืนข้อมูลมา ไม่ใช่พังแล้ว error (ดู #10):

```
forum_messages  0000_unknown_viper.sql:44-56    ไม่มี tenant_id
supersede_log   0003_rapid_strong_guy.sql:16-29 ไม่มี tenant_id
```

`supersede_log` เก็บ `old_title` `old_path` ของทุก tenant — audit log ที่รั่วข้าม tenant แย่กว่าไม่มี audit log เพราะคนเชื่อมัน

## คำถามที่ยังไม่ตัดสิน — `is_active` หรือ `tier`

ตอนนี้ tier 2 กับ tier 3 ใช้คนละ idiom และเพิ่งเห็นตอนวาด ASCII

```
memories.is_active   BOOL                        -- บิตเดียว
traces.status        raw | distilled | retired   -- pipeline
```

§3.2.1 ข้อ 3 เขียนไว้ว่า "two states need one bit, not a vocabulary" ซึ่งถูก แต่ tier 3 แหกกฎนี้ไปแล้ว และแหกถูก — trace มัน **เดินผ่าน state จริง** ส่วน memory ยังไม่ชัดว่าเดินหรือเปล่า

### ทำไมไม่เอาแบบ v3 ตรง ๆ

v3 มี tier แล้ว `core | warm | cold` พร้อม hysteresis สองทาง ส่วนนี้ทำมาดี แต่ที่ต่อสายไว้ผิด

```ts
// src/routes/memory/salience.ts
heat = visitScore*0.50 + accessRecency*0.24 + freshness*0.26
CORE_THRESHOLD 0.72 · WARM_THRESHOLD 0.22
CORE_HYSTERESIS 0.56 · COLD_HYSTERESIS 0.28
```

```
src/routes/memory/store.ts
  :146  reinforceRows   UPDATE ทุกแถวที่ค้นเจอ ทุกครั้งที่ recall
                        20 hits = 20 writes ต่อ 1 search
  :135  rebalance()     มี caller เดียว คือ :111 ตอนเปิดหน้า list tier
                        ไม่มี cron ไม่มี interval ไม่มี worker
  :90   includeCold ? undefined : ne(tier,'cold')   cold ไม่ถูกค้นเจอโดย default
```

ปัญหาจริงคือ: **decay ขับด้วย access แต่ access คือสิ่งที่ decay มีไว้ลงโทษ**

memory ที่ไม่มีใครเรียกใช้ → `last_accessed_at` ไม่เคยถูกแตะ → ไม่เคยคำนวณใหม่ → ไม่เคยถูก demote แถวที่ควรถูกลืมที่สุด คือแถวที่โค้ดไปไม่ถึง

หลักฐานอีกชิ้นในโค้ดเดียวกัน ชี้คนละทาง:

```ts
// src/openapi/memory.ts:170
function confidenceStrategy(): Spec {
  return { stored: false, strategy: 'query-time-confidence',
           signals: ['match_score','freshness_decay','usage_count','last_accessed_at'] }; }
```

confidence คำนวณตอน query ไม่เก็บอะไรเลย · heat คำนวณตอน read เก็บสี่คอลัมน์ สัญญาณชนิดเดียวกัน คำตอบตรงข้ามกัน อยู่ใน codebase เดียว — ฝั่ง query-time คือฝั่งที่อยู่รอด

### สามทางที่เหลือ

```
A · เก็บสองแกน       is_active BOOL + tier core|warm|cold
                     2 คอลัมน์ 9 state combination ~4 อันไม่มีความหมาย
                     is_active=false + tier='core'  ← อันนี้คืออะไร
                     §3.2.1 ไม่ต้องแก้

B · tier แทน is_active    tier core|warm|cold|retired
                     1 คอลัมน์ 1 predicate:  WHERE tier != 'cold'
                     ตรงกับที่ v3 ทำอยู่แล้วที่ store.ts:90
                     traces.status เป็น precedent tier 2/3 อ่านเหมือนกัน
                     ต้องแก้ §3.2.1 ข้อ 3 เขียน exception ให้ชัด
                     ⚠ คนกด unpublish กับ sweep เขียนคอลัมน์เดียวกัน
                       = two writers one fact = สิ่งที่ §14.4 ห้าม

C · แยกคนเขียน        tier เขียนโดย sweep เท่านั้น
                     is_active เป็น gate ของคนไม่ใช่ state
                     is_active=false override tier ทั้งหมด
```

ข้อโต้แย้งของ B โผล่ตอนวาด ASCII นี่แหละ ไม่ได้เห็นตอนคิดในหัว

**คำถามที่ต้องตอบก่อนเลือก: "unpublish memory" มีจริงไหมในระบบ** ถ้าไม่มีอะไรเรียกใช้ `is_active` เลย — มันติดมาจาก `sessions.is_active` ของ Honcho เฉย ๆ — B สะอาดทันที ข้อโต้แย้งหายไปเอง

---

## English summary

Same content, one line per section, for anyone who needs to skim it.

- **Three tiers, one shape.** Tier 1 is Honcho's five tables byte-compatible (additions are nullable only); tier 2 is v3's memory layer; tier 3 is activity. Tiers 2 and 3 were rewritten in tier 1's column idiom.
- **Column idiom.** `id` + `name` + `workspace_name` + two JSON bags + `created_at` + `UNIQUE(name, workspace_name)`. The test for any new field is **filter key or display field** — you `WHERE` on columns, and neither libSQL nor Lance pushes predicates into JSON. That test is why `memories` is 15 columns rather than 21.
- **Composite FKs are the isolation guarantee**, not a convention: the tenant rides inside every key, so a cross-bank reference is a constraint violation at INSERT. v3 used a runtime assertion and had two holes that failed *open* (#10).
- **The open fork.** `memories.is_active` is a bit while `traces.status` is already a three-state pipeline. Option A keeps both axes and admits meaningless state combinations; B lets `tier` replace `is_active` but puts two writers on one column, which §14.4 bans; C splits them, making `is_active` a human gate that overrides tier. Gated on a prior question: **does "unpublish a memory" exist as a real operation, or was `is_active` inherited from Honcho's `sessions` and never used?** If nothing calls it, B is clean.
- **Why not copy v3's tiers directly:** v3's hysteresis is good work, but `reinforceRows` writes on every read (20 hits = 20 UPDATEs per search) and `rebalance()` has one caller — the tier browser. So decay is access-driven, and access is exactly what decay exists to punish: the rows most in need of demotion are the ones the code never visits.

Design argument continues in #12 · decision tracked in #2

nodes.title: Feature Request: Multi-tenancy through dynamic bindings
nodes.body:
I am looking to manage multiple independent sites from a single EmDash installation/monorepo. Currently, EmDash appears focused on single-instance deployments. For devs managing dozens of client sites/properties, maintaining separate deployments for each site increases DevOps overhead and complicates global updates.

I would like to see native multi-tenancy support (similar to Payload CMS), allowing a single EmDash instance to:

- Identify tenants via domain name or request headers.

- Isolate data using either a shared database with tenantID scoping or separate D1 databases per tenant.

- Shared Codebase: Update the core CMS logic in one place (the monorepo/Worker) and have it reflect across all tenant sites immediately.

- Tenant-specific Configuration: Allow different themes or plugin settings based on the active tenant.

nodes.title: [Idea]: RFC: Ray Serve LLM Governance Middleware Integration
nodes.body:
### Your Idea

A community contributor (@Divyam19) volunteered on [Ray issue #65259](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65259#issuecomment-5253733728) to implement a governance middleware layer for Ray Serve LLM. They proposed TealTiger as the reference integration behind a backend-agnostic `LLMMiddleware` interface in Ray.

This discussion is to collaborate on the interface design before submitting an RFC/PR to Ray.


**Proposed architecture:**

1. **`LLMMiddleware` interface (lives in Ray)** — typed hooks at the semantic LLM request layer:
   - `before_inference(request, context) → request | BlockedResponse`
   - `after_inference(request, response, context) → response`
   - `on_stream_chunk(chunk, context) → chunk | None` (optional)

2. **`ray-tealtiger` package (lives here)** — reference implementation wrapping TealTiger's engine behind the interface. PII scanning, cost budgets, model access policies, audit receipts. Zero-LLM governance path.

**Open design questions for the RFC:**
- Where should hooks run — ingress/router level, per-model server level, or both?
- How to handle streaming responses (chunk-by-chunk vs full-response audit)?
- Configuration scope — app-level global policies vs per-model `LLMConfig.middleware`?




### Category

Integration

### What problem does this solve?


Ray Serve LLM has no built-in governance/guardrails layer. Teams in regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) currently have to either build custom deployments from scratch or add a separate proxy in front of Ray — losing all benefits of LLMRouter, autoscaling, and multi-model management. A middleware layer lets them use the standard `LLMConfig` pipeline with governance built in.


### Potential Impact

- Any team deploying LLMs on Ray in production (regulated or multi-tenant)
- Ray Serve LLM gets a governance story without building one in-house
- TealTiger gets a high-visibility integration (Ray has 43K+ stars)


### Implementation Thoughts


- TealTiger already works as ASGI middleware — adapting to typed `LLMMiddleware` hooks is straightforward
- We provide: PII patterns, governance policy schema, TEEC receipt format, ENFORCE/MONITOR/OBSERVE modes
- Ray provides: the hook interface, pipeline integration, streaming contract
- Keeps Ray from taking a hard dependency on any vendor

### Examples or References


- [Ray issue #65259](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/65259) — original proposal
- [Ray Discuss: preprocessing in Ray Serve LLM](https://discuss.ray.io/t/preprocessing-in-ray-serve-llm/23346) — community demand
- AG2 integration (PR #3128) — similar pattern: typed middleware interface in the framework, TealTiger as a pluggable extension
- LangChain middleware listing — same approach, framework-native hook + TealTiger adapter

nodes.title: Support metadata filters for RAG retrieval in /api/chat/completions
nodes.body:
Add support for passing metadata filters (payload filters) to the RAG retrieval pipeline through the `/api/chat/completions` API.

This would allow applications to leverage metadata already stored in vector databases (Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, etc.) without creating and managing a large number of Knowledge Collections.

---

## Motivation

Many enterprise applications need to restrict retrieval based on metadata such as:

* Access Control Lists (ACL)
* Tenant ID
* Department
* Project
* Workspace
* Repository
* Language
* Document type
* Business domain

Today, the only way to limit retrieval from the API is to provide a list of `files` or `collections`.

This works well for small deployments but becomes difficult to scale when an application contains hundreds or thousands of logical workspaces.

For example:

* 5,000 workspaces
* 200,000 documents
* millions of chunks

Creating one Knowledge Collection per workspace is not an ideal architecture.

Most vector databases already provide efficient metadata filtering during similarity search.

---

## Proposed API

Example:

```json
{
  "model": "mistral",
  "messages": [
    {
      "role": "user",
      "content": "Where is the Finance Department located?"
    }
  ],
  "files": [
    {
      "type": "collection",
      "id": "company_documents"
    }
  ],
  "retrieval": {
    "top_k": 20,
    "reranker_top_k": 10,
    "filter": {
      "must": [
        {
          "key": "workspaceId",
          "match": {
            "any": [
              "workspace-42",
              "workspace-81"
            ]
          }
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}
```

The backend would translate this filter into the native filtering mechanism of the configured vector database.

---

## Benefits

### Better scalability

Instead of:

* 5,000 Knowledge Collections

Applications could use:

* 1 Knowledge Collection
* metadata filtering

---

### Better performance

Vector databases optimize metadata filtering internally.

This avoids querying thousands of collections and improves retrieval quality.

---

### Enterprise security

Many enterprise applications already maintain their own permission system.

Applications could compute the list of accessible repositories or workspaces and pass it directly as a metadata filter.

The vector database would never return unauthorized chunks.

---

### Generic solution

This is not specific to ACLs.

The same mechanism could be used for:

* tenant isolation
* workspace selection
* project filtering
* language filtering
* document lifecycle
* document classification
* date ranges
* custom application metadata

---

## Compatibility

This feature would be fully backward compatible.

If no retrieval filter is provided, the current behavior remains unchanged.

---

## Possible implementation

The retrieval layer already knows which vector database is configured.

The backend could simply forward the provided filter to the underlying vector store implementation.

For example:

* Qdrant → Payload Filter
* Weaviate → Where Filter
* Milvus → Expression
* Elasticsearch → Bool Query

Each backend already supports metadata filtering natively.

---

## Why this matters

OpenWebUI is increasingly used as the conversational layer on top of enterprise knowledge systems.

Adding metadata filters would significantly improve:

* scalability
* security
* integration with existing document management systems
* multi-tenant deployments

while keeping the API simple and fully backward compatible.

nodes.title: Is it good to store user-created data in another collection than system-data?
nodes.body:
Hey everyone!

I am currently planning on creating a RAG application using Langchain4J and I would like to get some input. The system will have two kinds of data: 

1. Data provided by the system. This can be a a manual or other documents. It is data that will be cleaned up, split into chunks and ingested into qdrant. It might be a good idea to prepare all this data during development (or through some pipeline).

2. Data created by the user of the application. Users are able to create articles (e.g FAQ-texts) which we want to also add into our RAG data. If a user deletes such an article, we can delete it from qdrant, modify it etc.

Now when there is an update to the software, there might also be a new version of the manual and related data, which we will have to update then. (Maybe by delivering a new qdrant-snapshot file to replace the old collection or having some scripts to replace the data in the collection). 

I thought about creating two collections: one for the users data and one for the systems data. The FAQ says that having multiple collections might be considered an antipattern: https://qdrant.tech/documentation/faq/qdrant-fundamentals/#how-many-collections-can-i-create

So I would like to get some input if that is a terrible idea or a valid plan for my use case. Are there problems with delivering qdrant-snapshots for data updates?

nodes.title: Platform aggregator approach for SMB merchants in Korea — ACP integration guidance
nodes.body:
Hi ACP team and community,

I'm an individual developer based in South Korea, exploring building a multi-protocol commerce gateway that abstracts ACP (and UCP) for Korean SMB merchants who don't have engineering bandwidth to implement either protocol directly.

I've reviewed the spec, the OpenAI getting-started docs at developers.openai.com/commerce, and applied through the ACP product feed onboarding form. While waiting on that, I have a few questions that affect architecture decisions.

## Questions

**1. Aggregator/platform model for multiple merchants**

The spec describes a single business implementing checkout endpoints. For a platform that hosts many downstream merchants (similar to how Stripe's ACP implementation serves Stripe-using merchants):

- Is there an established pattern for a single ACP-implementing platform to represent multiple merchant identities to ChatGPT? Or is each merchant expected to apply independently?
- If platform aggregation is supported, what's the recommended way to model merchant identity in checkout sessions and webhook lifecycle events?

**2. ChatGPT activation for non-US merchants**

For UCP, AI Mode is currently US-only. ACP/ChatGPT Instant Checkout appears to have broader availability since ChatGPT itself is global. To confirm:

- Are there geographic restrictions on which merchants can be approved for ChatGPT product feed onboarding?
- For Korean merchants specifically, are there known examples already live, or would we be among the first?

**3. Stripe SPT vs alternative PSPs**

The reference implementation uses Stripe Shared Payment Token. In Korea, most SMB merchants use local PG providers (토스페이먼츠, KG이니시스, NHN KCP, Naver Pay) rather than Stripe. Reading the payment_handlers RFC, it seems custom handlers are possible.

- Is there guidance or precedent for defining payment handlers for non-Stripe PSPs?
- Is the seller-backed payment handler (rfc.seller_backed_payment_handler.md) the right path for merchants who want to use their existing local PG instead of Stripe SPT?
- Has anyone in the community implemented this for non-US markets?

**4. Compatibility with future UCP integration**

ACP and UCP have overlapping scopes but different governance. For a gateway intending to support both:

- Are there community recommendations for unified architecture (single product feed → both protocols, or maintain separate pipelines)?
- The agorio project (mentioned in this repo's discussions) seems to target this multi-protocol pattern — is that a reasonable reference?

## What I'm not asking

Not asking for early access or special treatment. Just trying to understand what's supported by design vs. what's possible but unusual, before committing to architecture. Happy to share more about the Korean SMB context if useful.

Thanks for the work — the protocol is well-specified and the active community here is encouraging.

— Sejin

nodes.title: Typed read-through caching decorators with compile-time tenancy safety
nodes.body:
`protoc-gen-cache` generates typed, read-through caching decorators for data access stores generated by `protoc-gen-store`. By reading `cache.v1` annotations alongside standard AIP resource definitions, the generator constructs caching layers that implement the identical Go store interfaces used by your application logic. Application handlers interact with the same `<Model>StoreIface` whether caching is enabled or omitted, preventing cache mechanics from leaking into business domains.

The initial release introduces the core generator plugin, the `cache.v1` annotation schema, compile-time validation for multi-tenant keyspace isolation, cross-store invalidation edges, and direct integration with `runtime-go/cache`.

## The problem with application-layer caching

Implementing caching directly inside application services or database access layers reliably introduces four classic engineering failures:

1. Cache stampedes: Concurrent misses on a hot or expired key trigger hundreds of simultaneous downstream database queries for identical data, degrading database performance under high load.
2. Absent negative caching: Requests for non-existent records repeatedly bypass the cache, forcing full store queries on every read attempt and leaving services vulnerable to denial-of-service patterns.
3. Reader starvation during expiry: Expired keys block downstream readers while synchronous reloading takes place, causing latency spikes on critical execution paths.
4. Stale invalidation drift: Invalidation routines written manually inside mutation handlers inevitably drift over time as secondary paths, bulk operations, or related child updates bypass manual purge hooks.

Low-level mechanics—such as singleflight grouping, negative caching markers, soft expiration with stale serving, and key formatting—are handled uniformly by the companion `runtime-go/cache` engine. What a generic runtime cannot know, however, is the structural reality of the domain: which entities map to which tables, how secondary lookup fields are indexed, which parent relationships establish tenant boundaries, and which mutations must evict related entries.

`protoc-gen-cache` extracts this information from protocol buffer schemas and generates Go decorators that wire runtime caching capabilities directly into store calls.

## Compile-time tenancy isolation

A database store enforces multi-tenant boundaries and row-level access control through query construction: applying `WHERE tenant_id = ?` filters, tenant-scoped joins, or connection-level row-level security. However, a read-through cache evaluates requests before the backing store is consulted. On a cache hit, the backing store never runs, and its security filters are completely bypassed.

If a nested resource is cached without explicitly binding parent segments into its cache key, records belonging to distinct parent entities will occupy the same cache key. A lookup for an entity under tenant B will successfully retrieve the cached payload previously loaded by tenant A.

To prevent this vulnerability, `protoc-gen-cache` validates resource definitions against their AIP patterns at code generation time. If a message specifies a nested pattern such as `users/{user}/documents/{document}`, the generator requires a field carrying the parent reference to be annotated with `(cache.v1.cache_scope)`.

If an AIP pattern contains an unbound parent variable, code generation halts immediately with a compiler error:

```console
$ buf generate
cache: tenancy.v1.Document: the resource pattern "users/{user}/documents/{document}"
       nests this resource under {user}, but no field binds that segment into the
       cache namespace.

       A cache answers before the store is consulted, so on a hit the store's
       row-level scoping never runs. With {user} unbound, every parent's entries
       share one keyspace and the first hit serves whichever was cached first —
       one tenant reading another's rows. This is the one thing this generator
       refuses to emit.
```

The plugin deliberately emits a hard generation error rather than a warning. Emitting code with unbound parents allows silent data leakage across tenant boundaries; halting generation guarantees that unsecured cache configurations cannot be compiled into production binaries.

## Generation pipeline and shared intermediate representations

`protoc-gen-cache` operates as a downstream stage in the code generation toolchain, executing after `protoc-gen-store`. Its execution requires no direct coupling between the plugins beyond sharing a consistent data dictionary and an imported Go path:

```yaml
version: v2
plugins:
  - local: protoc-gen-store
    out: generated/gorm
    opt:
      - target=gorm
      - stores=true
      - go_module=github.com/example/service/generated/gorm

  - local: protoc-gen-cache
    out: generated/cache
    opt:
      - store_module=github.com/example/service/generated/gorm
```

The `stores=true` option instructs `protoc-gen-store` to emit `<Model>StoreIface` interfaces. `protoc-gen-cache` consumes these definitions and generates concrete wrapper types that satisfy them. Because both generators utilize the shared `protokit` engine to inspect protocol buffer schemas, they reach deterministic agreement on table names, primary keys, schema namespaces, and field types without runtime coordination.

Application wiring replaces the raw store pointer with the generated decorator during service initialization:

```go
scope := bookstorev1cache.BookScope{AuthorID: authorID}
db, err := bookstorev1cache.OpenBookCache(ctx, cacheProvider, scope)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}

// cachedStore satisfies BookstoreIface
cachedStore, err := bookstorev1cache.NewCachedBookStore(
    ctx,
    underlyingStore,
    db,
    scope,
    bookstorev1cache.BookEdges{
        Author: authorStore,
    },
)
```

Callers consume `cachedStore` through the standard interface, leaving business logic decoupled from cache maintenance.

## Key layout architecture

Keys emitted by the runtime and generator avoid global string concatenations. Every cache key is split into three explicitly owned segments:

```
mycompany:prod : bookstore.v1.book.author.a-123 : cache:idx:by:isbn:9780441013593
──────────────   ──────────────────────────────   ────────────────────────────────
Config.Prefix           protoc-gen-cache               runtime-go/cache/core
Deployment scope       Tenancy namespace                  Keyspace layout
```

1. Deployment prefix: Owned by deployment configuration. Isolates application instances, environments, or preview stacks from one another within a shared cache cluster.
2. Resource namespace: Owned by `protoc-gen-cache`. Formed from the protocol buffer resource name and all bound `cache_scope` segments. Scopes operations to a specific entity type and tenant parent.
3. Keyspace and indexing layout: Owned exclusively by `runtime-go/cache/core`. Defines storage structure for primary entries, secondary lookup tables, field tracking, and stale state flags.

Because the generator controls only the middle namespace segment, changing internal storage layouts within the runtime requires no regenerated protobuf wrappers, while tenant partition boundaries remain strictly enforced.

## Strategies and backend capabilities

`cache.v1` exposes four caching strategies, each mapping to discrete operational requirements in the data tier:

- `STRATEGY_ASIDE`: Standard read-through cache indexed by primary resource identifier. Entries are fetched on miss and held until expired or explicitly invalidated.
- `STRATEGY_INDEXED`: Maintains secondary lookup indices alongside primary records, allowing point lookups by unique secondary attributes (such as an ISBN or email) to resolve through the cache.
- `STRATEGY_DOCUMENT`: Primary key lookup supporting resource enumeration within a given namespace partition.
- `STRATEGY_VOLATILE`: Lightweight transient key storage bypassing durability hooks.

Backend providers differ significantly in their operational capabilities. Redis and Dragonfly support complex data structures including server-side sets and key scanning, making them capable of handling `INDEXED` and `DOCUMENT` strategies along with lock leases. memcached, by contrast, operates purely as a key-value store with bulk read support, lacking native sets and TTL-inspection operations required for lease-based stale windows.

Instead of failing silently or masking unsupported operations with expensive client-side emulation, the generated decorators assert runtime capabilities during initialization. If a service attempts to configure an `INDEXED` strategy against a backend driver that does not support set operations, initialization fails deterministically at startup.

## Cross-store invalidation edges

Data models frequently require changes in one store to invalidate cached views in another. For example, creating or deleting a `Book` record modifies the aggregate inventory or author record representing the parent entity.

`cache.v1` allows annotations to define invalidation edges connecting dependent resources. When mutations occur on the child store, the generated decorator automatically fires edge events across configured store interfaces, evicting the affected parent cache entries without requiring cross-domain application code.

## Next steps

The `protoc-gen-cache` compiler binary is distributed through Homebrew and Go toolchains. Protocol buffer annotations are published through the Buf Schema Registry at `buf.build/the-protobuf-project/cache`. Detailed examples demonstrating store decoration, secondary index resolution, and edge invalidation are available in the repository's example suite.

## Contributors

- [@oh-tarnished](https://github.com/oh-tarnished)


---

Published at [https://the-protobuf-project.org/announcements/cache-v0-1-0](https://the-protobuf-project.org/announcements/cache-v0-1-0).

nodes.title: project quality checks please
nodes.body: ## Project Quality Checks Every dbt project starts off as a blank slate. Clean. Organized. Governed. And then, the project grows. And grows. And grows. And as you add more models and more contributors, things start to slip through the cracks. A new model is added that doesn’t *quite* fit your org’s naming convention. A new column is added, but is missing a `description`. A model is promoted to `public`, but doesn’t get an assigned `owner`. This slow degradation of project quality happens silently in dbt today. There are many community-driven packages and extensions of dbt that attempt to fill this gap — enabling teams to enforce project quality and alert developers when expectations drift from reality: [dbt-checkpoint](https://github.com/dbt-checkpoint/dbt-checkpoint), @VDFaller’s [metadata_checks](https://github.com/VDFaller/jaffle_shop_duckdb/tree/dbt-wizard/metadata_checks), [dbt-artifacts](https://github.com/brooklyn-data/dbt_artifacts), [dbt-doctor](https://github.com/northgraindata/dbt-doctor), [dblect](https://github.com/dvryaboy/dblect/), [dbt-debt](https://github.com/obrienciaran/dbt-debt), [tff](https://github.com/tjirab/tff), [dbt-bouncer](https://github.com/godatadriven/dbt-bouncer), [sdf’s checks](https://docs.sdf.com/guide/data-quality/checks), the list goes on… [The proof is out there](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt13951868/). And project quality is every-growing in importance as code contributions are exploding in the age of AI. As a creator and maintainer of one of those packages ([dbt-project-evaluator](https://dbt-labs.github.io/dbt-project-evaluator/latest/) 👽), I know both a) how important this feature is for maintaining a high-quality dbt project and b) how dbt isn’t-quite built for this today. [The way dbt-project-evaluator tackles this problem](https://dbt-labs.github.io/dbt-project-evaluator/latest/#how-it-works) is by unpacking the jinja `{{ graph }}` variable into a series of models and then adding a data test to each model checking for alignment with dbt best practices. And I’ll be the first to say that while this is clever and does indeed work, it’s a bit of a pain. These checks can *only* be run after those “core metadata” models have been built, and we don’t have a clean way to slowly introduce checks to an existing problematic project (e.g. there’s no simple mechanism to say “does *this* PR add a new problem or not?”). So the pattern goes… the community has identified a problem, has extended dbt is fun-and-freaky ways to solve it, and now… it’s time to build a *better* out-of-the-box solution directly into dbt. Why now? Hopefully you’ve seen the announcement of dbt Core v2 (if not, go check out [the blog post](https://docs.getdbt.com/blog/dbt-core-v2-is-here?version=2.0&name=Fusion) ;))! or the github discussions on our [re-vamp of dbt-docs](https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-core/discussions/13080) and [writing to agents schema directly from dbt](https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-core/discussions/15447) 👀 The key piece that’s relevant for this discussion is that **v2 writes our your project metadata as new parquet artifacts** — a high-performance alternative to large JSON files that can be directly queried through DuckDB. We’ve been calling this the “index layer” (though I’ve started thinking of it as “the dbt information schema”), and you can check it out [here](https://github.com/dbt-labs/dbt-core/tree/main/crates/dbt-index-core). This layer is critical into bringing “project quality checks” to life. So what might that look like? We think: [*it’s all just SQL*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turtles_all_the_way_down). **Any assertion you can express as a SQL query against your project's metadata should be enforceable as a first-class “check” in dbt.** Let’s say you want to ensure every public model has an `owner` defined in its YAML. You write that “check” as a SQL query against the “dbt information schema”: ```sql -- SPEC IS TBD select unique_id, name from {{ info_schema('nodes') }} where resource_type = 'model' and access = 'public' and owner IS NULL ``` Just like tests, by default a check that returns 0 rows is a `success`; if any rows are returned, it’s an `error`. Unlike tests, these can run after `compile` without ever touching your data warehouse. 🔥 ## Requirements *Here’s what I’m thinking:* - checks should be defined in SQL (just like data tests!) - checks should query your project metadata (”the dbt information schema” parquets to disk) - checks should work with `state:modified` and other selectors to only evaluate a subset of your project - you should be able to prevent commands from running based on the results of checks - you should be able to disable checks installed from a dbt package ## Open Questions Ok, that’s the big vision! There is a lot to sort out for how this should all work, and I know there are a *ton* of community members out there that have built or thought-about-building a solution for this. So please, chime in with your thoughts! Here’s the open questions already in my brain: 1. Should checks be a (1) **new node type** or a (2) **new test type**? (2) makes use of existing commands, configs, env vars, etc, but “checks” aren’t associated with a specific model/node, the way that tests are. 🤔 option 1: new node type - Checks are a new node type in you DAG. - Checks are `.sql` files in a `checks/` directory. - You can customize that directory by configuring `check-paths:` in your `dbt_project.yml`. - Checks are run via `dbt check` command (a la [`dbt lint`](https://docs.getdbt.com/reference/commands/lint)). - Or (maybe?) as a part of `dbt build` executed in appropriate DAG-order (”as early as possible”). Or as part of `dbt compile`. Exclude checks with `resource_type:` selector. option 2: new test type - `metadata_tests` (name TBD) are assertions you make about the *metadata* in your project. - `dbt tests` runs all test types. You can use existing `test_type:` selector / environment variable to optionally exclude / include specific test types (e.g. exclude unit tests in production environment). - `dbt build` includes all tests, executed in appropriate DAG-order (”as early as possible”). - Set `severity` (and `warn_if`/`error_if` thresholds) to control what logs/status should be outputted by a failing test. - Set `fail calc` to control how failures are evaluated. 2. When should checks run? `dbt check`, `dbt compile`, `dbt lint`, `dbt build`? 3. How should users specify modeling layers, naming conventions, etc. that will be used as part of checks? Should we have a set default? dbt-project-evaluator makes uses of [project variables](https://dbt-labs.github.io/dbt-project-evaluator/latest/customization/overriding-variables/#dag-variables), but we could (should?) do something that feels more clean. ```yaml layers: - name: staging prefixes: ['stg_'] folders: ['staging'] - name: marts prefixes: ['fct_', 'dim_'] folders: ['marts'] ... ``` 4. Beyond the checks framework, should dbt also ship with basic built-in checks or should that be handled by a package (a la `dbt_utils` for data tests)? If we did include basic built-in checks how would you “turn them on”? 5. What “rules” should be handled by `lint` vs. checks? 6. Do folks want additional jinja in these checks beyond “ref”-ing the dbt information schema (like `run_query()`, `{% if ... %}`, `etc.)`? 7. What kind of logging do you want these checks to produce? 8. What should the default severity be of checks? Should that be configurable? How?

nodes.title: Can an LLM Security Proxy Become the Missing Control Plane for Multi-Provider AI?
nodes.body:
Many teams now use more than one model provider, plus internal tools, RAG pipelines, and custom agents.

That creates a messy security problem:
- controls vary by provider
- logs are fragmented
- policies drift across services
- incidents become hard to reconstruct

Does this create a need for a single inline security control plane for multi-provider AI systems?

Or is a central proxy model too blunt for real-world applications?

nodes.title: feat(source-mssql): Add Microsoft Entra ID Service Principal Authentication Support
nodes.body:
## Summary

This discussion proposes adding Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal` authentication as a **non-breaking** option for the MSSQL source connector, leveraging the JDBC driver's native support.

### Related Issues
- [#9557](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/issues/9557) — "[source-MSSQL] Support Windows authentication" (22+ upvotes, frozen)
- [#20866](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/issues/20866) — "Source MSSQL - Failed to load MSAL4J Java library for performing ActiveDirectoryPassword authentication" (frozen)
- [Community PR #61547](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/pull/61547) — Previous community attempt (closed during CDK migration)

### Prior Art (Closed PR)
A reference implementation was developed in [PR #74904](https://github.com/airbytehq/airbyte/pull/74904) (now closed) on branch `devin/1773700827-mssql-entra-id-auth`. The code changes are preserved there for reference.

---

## Motivation

Multiple users across issues #9557 and #20866 have stated that the lack of Entra ID / non-SQL-password authentication is a **dealbreaker** for their organizations:

> *"Lack of this feature disqualifies Airbyte as a candidate for our organization (big Danish governmental organization)."*

> *"For organizations heavy on MSSQL, it makes the entire Airbyte software kind of a non-starter."*

Many enterprises require Entra ID authentication for Azure SQL Database / Azure Synapse Analytics and cannot use SQL Server authentication for security compliance reasons.

---

## Proposed Approach

### Leverage JDBC Driver's Native Support

The MSSQL JDBC driver (`mssql-jdbc:12.10.1`) already supports Entra ID authentication natively via the `authentication` connection property. The `azure-identity:1.15.3` dependency is **already present** in the connector's `build.gradle`. No new dependencies are needed.

### Non-Breaking Design

Add an **optional** `authentication` oneOf selector to the connector spec (following the existing `EncryptionSpecification` sealed interface pattern):

- **`sql_password`** (default) — username + password (current behavior, fully backward compatible)
- **`active_directory_service_principal`** (new) — tenant_id + client_id + client_secret

When no `authentication` block is present in the config, the connector falls back to top-level `username`/`password` fields — **zero disruption to existing connections**.

### JDBC Property Mapping

| Auth Method | JDBC Properties Set |
|---|---|
| SQL Password (current) | `user` = username, `password` = password |
| Service Principal (new) | `user` = client_id, `password` = client_secret, `authentication` = `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipal`, `tenantId` = tenant_id |

### Implementation Details

The reference implementation (branch `devin/1773700827-mssql-entra-id-auth`) touches three files:

1. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfigurationSpecification.kt`**
   - Makes `username`/`password` fields nullable (from `lateinit var` to `var String? = null`)
   - Adds `AuthenticationSpecification` sealed interface with `SqlPasswordAuthentication` and `ActiveDirectoryServicePrincipalAuthentication` variants
   - Adds `@JsonSetter`/`@JsonGetter` methods for the optional `authentication` block
   - Adds `MicronautPropertiesFriendlyAuthenticationSpecification` for Micronaut DI compatibility

2. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfiguration.kt`**
   - Updates the factory to check for `authenticationJson` and set JDBC properties accordingly
   - Falls back to top-level `username`/`password` when no auth block is present

3. **`MsSqlServerSourceConfigurationSpecificationTest.kt`**
   - Adds tests for backward compatibility, SQL password auth block, and service principal auth block

### Why Not OAuth/Consent Flow?

The Azure Blob Storage connector uses a platform-level OAuth consent flow (`MicrosoftAzureBlobStorageOAuthFlow.kt` in `airbyte-platform-internal`). This approach was evaluated but is **not recommended** for MSSQL because:
- The JDBC driver handles token acquisition internally — manually managing tokens would fight the driver's architecture
- It would require changes in both the connector repo AND `airbyte-platform-internal`
- Service Principal auth is the enterprise standard for machine-to-machine workloads like data pipelines
- No other JDBC-based Airbyte connector uses a platform-side OAuth consent flow

### Future Extensions

Phase 2 could add:
- `ActiveDirectoryDefault` — uses `DefaultAzureCredential` (managed identity for Azure-hosted Airbyte)
- `ActiveDirectoryPassword` — Entra username + password (deprecated by Microsoft but still supported)
- User-delegated OAuth consent flow (if demand justifies the cross-repo complexity)

---

## Open Questions

1. **Version bump**: Should this be a patch bump (4.3.6) or minor bump (4.4.0)? The change is additive and non-breaking.
2. **SpotBugs**: The reference implementation triggered SpotBugs warnings due to nullable `username`/`password` fields. Need to add appropriate `@SuppressFBWarnings` annotations or restructure.
3. **JSON schema ordering**: The `authentication` field uses `"order":4`, which may collide with the existing `username` field. May need adjustment.
4. **Documentation**: What level of docs changes are needed? (connector docs, migration guide, etc.)

---

nodes.title: Multi-Harness Agent Platform
nodes.body:
# Multi-Harness Agent Platform â€” Full Architecture & Implementation Plan

## 1. Vision

Build a multi-tenant platform that allows users to:

- Discover and install multiple AI agent harnesses.
- Pin and manage harness versions and immutable runtime artifacts.
- Start many concurrent sessions across different harnesses.
- Run different harnesses simultaneously for different tasks.
- Select models independently from harnesses and providers.
- Connect MCP servers and manage short-lived OAuth/access tokens.
- Surface native harness commands, capabilities, notifications, compaction, memory, plugins, and extensions through a dynamic UI.
- Persist conversations, session state, memory, workspaces, artifacts, and checkpoints.
- Run untrusted/long-running agents in isolated runtimes.
- Track usage, cost, audit events, approvals, and operational health.
- Add new harnesses through a stable adapter SDK and conformance test suite.

The core architectural principle is:

> Normalize the platform-level lifecycle and security model, but do not force every harness into the same internal implementation.

---

# 2. Supported Harnesses

Initial catalog:

- [Pi](https://github.com/badlogic/pi-mono) â€” Minimal and highly extensible agent harness with an agent runtime, tools, sessions, and a coding-agent CLI.
- [OpenHarness](https://github.com/hotsun/openharness) â€” Open-source agent harness focused on tools, skills, memory, plugins, permissions, and multi-agent workflows.
- [jcode](https://github.com/Ravi-bit-app/jcode) â€” Coding-agent harness designed around efficient multi-session workflows and extensibility.
- [Grok CLI](https://github.com/xai-org/grok-cli) â€” General-purpose terminal agent from xAI for coding and agentic workflows.
- [OpenCode](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode) â€” Open-source terminal coding agent with an extensible architecture and support for multiple model providers.
- [Goose](https://github.com/block/goose) â€” Extensible open-source agent with tools, extensions, and MCP integration.
- [OpenHands](https://github.com/OpenHands/OpenHands) â€” Autonomous software-development platform providing agents with coding, terminal, browser, and task-execution capabilities.
- [SWE-agent](https://github.com/SWE-agent/SWE-agent) â€” Agent framework focused on autonomously solving software-engineering tasks and GitHub issues.

# 3. Core Architectural Principles

## 3.1 Harness != Model != Provider != Credential != Runtime

Keep these independent:

```text
Harness
  |
  +-- Harness Version
  |
  +-- Adapter Version
  |
  +-- Runtime Artifact
  |
  +-- Model Configuration
        |
        +-- Provider
        |
        +-- Credential
```

## 3.2 Control Plane vs Data Plane

### Control Plane

Responsible for:

- Identity
- Tenants
- Users and teams
- Projects
- Harness registry
- Versions
- Installation configuration
- Model registry
- Policies
- Scheduling
- Quotas
- Billing
- Session metadata
- Configuration
- Audit

### Data Plane

Responsible for:

- Runtime containers/VMs
- Harness processes
- MCP calls
- Tool execution
- Workspace access
- Agent execution
- Streaming events
- Artifacts

This separation is essential for scaling.

## 3.3 Immutable execution

Never run a production session from `latest`.

Resolve:

```text
harness + version
        |
        v
immutable artifact digest
```

Every execution stores the exact digest.

Support:

- OAuth/OIDC.

- Service accounts.

# 8. Harness Registry

The registry describes available harnesses.

Example:

```yaml
harness:
  id: pi
  name: Pi
  vendor: community

versions:
  - version: 0.9.2
    channel: stable
    status: supported

capabilities:
  sessions: true
  streaming: true
  commands: true
  mcp: true
  compaction: true
```

The registry should not contain only a list of names. It should also contain:

- Supported platforms
- Architectures
- Release channels
- Artifact metadata
- Runtime requirements
- Adapter compatibility
- Capabilities
- Configuration schema
- UI schema support
- Security requirements
- License metadata
- Health status
- Deprecation/EOL state

# 9. Harness Version and Binary Management

## Version hierarchy

There are independent versions:

```text
Platform Version
Harness Version
Adapter Version
Runtime Image Version
Plugin Version
MCP Protocol Version
```

Do not tie adapter version to harness version.

## Artifact model

Example:

```yaml
harness: pi
version: 0.9.2

artifact:
  type: container
  image: registry.example.com/harness/pi:0.9.2
  digest: sha256:abc123

platforms:
  - linux/amd64
  - linux/arm64
```

## Installation flow

```text
User selects harness/version
        |
        v
Version Resolver
        |
        v
Compatibility Check
        |
        v
Artifact Verification
        |
        v
Private Registry
        |
        v
Runtime Manager
```

Verify:

- SHA256 digest
- Artifact signature where available
- Source/release provenance
- License
- Security policy
- Runtime requirements

## Version channels

Support:

```text
stable
beta
nightly
```

## Version pinning

Store:

```json
{
  "harness": "pi",
  "version": "0.9.2",
  "artifact_digest": "sha256:abc123",
  "adapter_version": "2.1.0"
}
```

## Harness Lock

Projects should optionally contain:

```yaml
harnesses:
  pi:
    version: 0.9.2
    digest: sha256:abc123

  opencode:
    version: 0.8.3
    digest: sha256:def456
```

This provides reproducibility.

# 10. Runtime Management

Prefer containerized execution over installing all harnesses on the host.

```text
Worker Node
  |
  +-- Runtime: Pi 0.9.2
  +-- Runtime: Goose 1.2.1
  +-- Runtime: OpenCode 0.8.3
```

Runtime should support:

- Start
- Stop
- Pause where possible
- Resume
- Health checks
- Resource limits
- Network policy
- Secret injection
- Workspace mounting
- Artifact mounting
- Log collection
- Metrics
- Timeout
- Cleanup

Use a runtime abstraction so Docker/Kubernetes/VM execution can evolve independently.

# 12. Harness Adapter Architecture

Every harness should implement a platform adapter.

Conceptual interface:

```python
class HarnessAdapter:
    def metadata(self): ...
    def capabilities(self): ...

    def install(self): ...
    def start(self): ...
    def stop(self): ...

    def create_session(self): ...
    def resume_session(self): ...
    def terminate_session(self): ...

    def send_message(self): ...
    def stream_events(self): ...

    def list_commands(self): ...
    def execute_command(self): ...

    def list_tools(self): ...
    def configure_mcp(self): ...

    def get_state(self): ...
    def get_context(self): ...
    def compact(self): ...

    def get_memory(self): ...
    def get_plugins(self): ...

    def health(self): ...
```

The exact implementation varies by harness.

The platform owns the lifecycle contract.

# 24. MCP Architecture

Do not allow every harness to independently manage credentials.

Recommended:

```text

   v

   |

   +-- Credential Manager
   +-- OAuth Manager

   +-- Audit
   |
   v
MCP Server
```

Where native harness MCP behavior is required, the adapter can bridge it.

# 25. Short-Lived MCP Tokens

For a 5-minute token:

```text
Session
  |
  v
MCP Gateway
  |
  v
Token Cache
  |
  +-- valid -> use
  |
  +-- near expiry -> refresh
  |
  +-- expired -> refresh
  |
  v
MCP Server
```

Never store only a token expiry and hope the harness handles it.

Use:

```text
access_token
expires_at
refresh_token / refresh mechanism
provider
scope
credential_id
```

Token refresh should happen centrally when possible.

## Important

Use a safety margin, for example:

```text
expires_at - current_time < refresh_window
```

instead of waiting for the exact expiration second.

## Concurrent refresh protection

If 20 tool calls notice an expired token simultaneously:

```text
20 requests
    |
    v
single-flight refresh
    |
    v
new token
    |
    v
20 requests continue
```

Avoid a refresh storm.

```text
      v
Publish artifact
```

This is critical once you support dozens of harnesses.

---

# 51. Developer SDK

Provide an SDK for external harness adapters.

Conceptually:

```python
from platform_sdk import HarnessAdapter

class MyHarness(HarnessAdapter):
    ...
```

SDK should provide:

- Lifecycle interface
- Session interface
- Event interface
- Tool interface
- MCP bridge
- UI manifest
- Command schema
- Capability declaration
- Logging
- Metrics
- Tracing
- Secrets access
- Workspace API

---

# 52. API Design

Suggested API groups:

```text
/v1/auth/*

/v1/policies/*
```

Streaming:

```text
/ws/sessions/{session_id}
/ws/executions/{execution_id}
```

Or SSE where appropriate.

The frontend should never connect directly to arbitrary harness containers.

---

# 53. Example Session Start

```text
POST /v1/tasks
        |
        v
Authenticate
        |
        v
Authorize
        |
        v
Resolve harness
        |
        v
Resolve harness version
        |
        v
Resolve adapter
        |
        v
Resolve model
        |
        v
Resolve credentials
        |
        v
Resolve workspace
        |
        v
Check quota/policy
        |
        v
Schedule runtime
        |
        v
Start harness
        |
        v
Create session
        |
        v
Stream events
```

---

# 54. Example User Experience

## Harness Marketplace

```text
Pi
v0.9.2
Coding â€¢ MCP â€¢ Sessions

[Install]

OpenCode
v0.8.3
Coding â€¢ Multiple providers

[Install]
```

## Session

```text
+-----------------------------------------+
| OpenCode                    Running     |
+-----------------------------------------+
| Model: GPT                              |
| Context: 64%                            |
|                                         |
| Agent conversation                      |
|                                         |
| [user message]                          |
| [assistant message]                     |
|                                         |
| Tool execution                          |
|   github.search               âœ“         |
|   terminal                   running    |
+-----------------------------------------+
| /  Commands                             |
+-----------------------------------------+
```

The UI is driven by capabilities and schemas rather than hardcoded harness assumptions.

---

# 55. Database Model

Core tables/collections:

```text
tenants
users
teams
projects

conversations
messages
tasks
executions
sessions

harnesses
harness_versions
harness_installations
harness_adapters

usage_records
quotas

```

Do not put all harness-specific state into a giant universal table. Use metadata + JSON/document fields where appropriate.

---

# 56. Recommended Infrastructure

A practical starting stack:

```text
Frontend
  React / Next.js

API
  FastAPI

Primary DB
  PostgreSQL

Cache / ephemeral state
  Redis

Queue
  Redis Streams / RabbitMQ / Kafka / managed queue

Object Storage
  S3-compatible storage

Runtime
  Docker initially
  Kubernetes when scale requires it

Observability
  OpenTelemetry
  Prometheus
  Grafana
  centralized logs

Model Gateway
  LiteLLM or equivalent

Secrets
  Vault / cloud secrets manager

Container Registry
  OCI-compatible registry
```

Choose managed services where possible.

---

# 57. Initial Deployment Architecture

Do not start with dozens of microservices.

Start as a modular control-plane application:

```text
FastAPI
 |
 +-- auth module
 +-- project module
 +-- harness module
 +-- model module
 +-- session module
 +-- MCP module
 +-- plugin module
 +-- workspace module
 +-- billing module

```

Separate runtime workers:

```text
Queue
 |

Worker

```

Split services only when scaling pressure justifies it.

---

# 58. Scaling Strategy

## Stage 1 â€” MVP

```text
1 API
1 DB
1 Redis
1 worker pool
Docker
S3
WebSocket
```

Support:

- 2â€“3 harnesses
- Basic sessions
- MCP
- Model selection
- Basic UI

## Stage 2 â€” Production

Add:

- Horizontal API scaling
- Worker pools
- Distributed scheduler
- Usage metering

## Stage 3 â€” Large Scale

Add:

- Kubernetes
- Runtime warm pools

- Multi-region
- Regional queues
- Autoscaling
- Tenant isolation
- Advanced policy engine
- Enterprise SSO
- Advanced billing

---

# 59. Security Model

Security boundaries:

```text
Browser
  |
  v
API
  |
  v
Control Plane
  |
  v
Runtime Scheduler
  |
  v
Sandbox
  |
  v
Harness
  |
  +-- Tool
  +-- MCP
  +-- Network
  +-- Workspace
```

Principles:

- Default deny
- Least privilege
- Short-lived credentials
- Never expose raw secrets to UI
- Never trust harness output
- Isolate tenants
- Isolate workspaces
- Restrict network
- Verify artifacts
- Audit sensitive operations
- Require approval for destructive actions

---

# 60. Important Edge Cases

Design for:

- Harness crashes
- Container crashes
- Host crashes
- Model provider outage
- MCP server outage
- Token expiration during tool call
- Concurrent token refresh
- WebSocket disconnect
- User reconnect
- Duplicate API request
- Scheduler retry
- Queue message duplication
- Workspace corruption
- Artifact upload failure
- Partial tool execution
- Harness upgrade during active sessions
- Adapter incompatibility
- Model becomes unavailable
- Plugin incompatibility
- Quota reached mid-task
- User cancellation during tool execution
- Network partition
- Database failover

---

# 61. Upgrade Strategy

Never upgrade active sessions implicitly.

Example:

```text
Pi 0.9.2
 |
 +-- existing sessions -> stay on 0.9.2
 |
 +-- new sessions -> 0.10.0
```

Upgrade flow:

